strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the gap between static and continuous dynamic reconstruction methods for multi-period scenes with discontinuous changes
Novel dataset (ChronoScene) with 12 real and 6 synthetic scenes spanning long temporal gaps, providing a valuable benchmark for future research
Clear technical approach with explicit decomposition of period-invariant and period-specific components through temporally modulated Gaussians
Strong and consistent empirical results outperforming relevant baselines (3DGS, GS-W, 4DGS, Scaffold-GS) across multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, both qualitative and quantitative results on real and synthetic scenes
Detailed supplementary material with implementation details, hyperparameters, and extensive ablation studies on feature dimensions and initialization
Effective visual illustrations and qualitative comparisons demonstrating faithful reconstruction of period-specific geometry and appearance changes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily a combination of existing techniques (Gaussian splatting, temporal MLPs, photometric losses) rather than fundamentally new concepts
Insufficient temporal analysis: no systematic study of how performance degrades with temporal gap size, limiting understanding of practical applicability
No computational cost analysis provided: missing training time, inference speed, memory consumption comparisons with baselines
Modest dataset size (12 real scenes) with limited diversity—all real scenes are urban/aerial; generalization to indoor or natural scenes unclear
Incomplete baseline comparison: only 3DGS-based methods; missing comparisons with video NeRF, temporal NeRF, or image-based temporal methods
Anchor scaffold assumption not thoroughly analyzed: behavior under major geometric changes (demolition, major reconstruction) is not discussed
Missing failure case analysis and method limitations: no clear guidance on when the method struggles or conditions it cannot handle
Experimental design concerns: joint multi-period training (ChronoGS) versus independent per-period training (baselines) may not be entirely fair; no error bars or statistical significance testing
Synthetic scenes created via manual editing may not reflect realistic temporal changes; some design choices (e.g., K=10 Gaussians, photometric loss formulation) lack justification
No code release mentioned and inter-scene generalization not evaluated, limiting reproducibility and broader applicability assessment

strengths: Novel problem formulation and first comprehensive solution for multi-period scene reconstruction with discrete geometry and appearance changes
High-quality ChronoScene benchmark dataset with 12 scenes, 8,891 geo-tagged images, and documented temporal variations—valuable community resource
Well-motivated technical approach elegantly decomposing invariant (anchor scaffold) from period-varying components with clear presentation and effective figures
Comprehensive experimental validation with thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-4) justifying each component and consistent improvements across all metrics and scenes
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, released code, and public dataset availability
Strong empirical results outperforming multiple baselines (3DGS, Scaffold-GS, GS-W, 4DGS) while maintaining reasonable memory footprint
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—individual components (anchor scaffold, period-varying features, 3DGS) are largely borrowed; main contribution is integration rather than fundamental innovation
Missing temporal consistency metrics—no quantitative evaluation of temporal smoothness or interpolation quality between discrete periods despite this being central to the problem

Identifiability and theoretical justification lacking—no analysis of whether the invariant/period-varying decomposition is unique or optimal; no guidance on when the binary decomposition is sufficient
Dataset scope limited to 12 urban/aerial scenes—robustness to diverse environments (indoor, non-urban, extreme appearance changes) and different temporal resolutions unexplored

Incomplete baseline comparisons—no comparison with simpler alternatives (separate models per period, interpolation methods) and limited depth analyzing performance gaps with recent dynamic scene methods
No failure case analysis or discussion of method limitations—all presented scenes appear well-behaved; unclear when ChronoGS is preferable to alternatives or where it fails
Scalability concerns unaddressed—computational overhead vs. training K separate models, memory complexity with increasing periods, and training time comparisons absent

Technical clarity issues including insufficient detail on camera pose registration across periods, unclear explanation of time encoding design choices, and missing ablation on key threshold parameters (τ=0.5)

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem of multi-period 3D scene reconstruction with clear real-world applications
Novel technical contribution: temporal modulation mechanism for disentangling invariant and period-specific components within unified Gaussian framework
Comprehensive ablation studies clearly demonstrate value of each component; good experimental methodology with multiple metrics and baselines
Valuable dataset contribution (ChronoScene) addressing gap in available benchmarks with commitment to public release
Detailed implementation details and transparent experimental setup aid reproducibility; clear visual improvements over baselines in Figures 6-7
Solid mathematical formulation and optimization strategy with well-designed temporal encoding for smooth period transitions
weaknesses: Limited temporal scope: evaluation restricted to slow scene changes (seasonal/construction) in urban environments; unclear generalization to rapid changes, non-rigid deformations, or indoor scenes
Temporal interpolation evaluation incomplete: only qualitative results shown (Fig. 7); no quantitative metrics for intermediate period reconstruction quality
Computational efficiency not addressed: no training time comparisons, memory requirements, or scalability analysis to more periods despite storing multiple Gaussian sets
Insufficient dynamic method comparison: only limited comparison with 4DGS; marginal quantitative improvements over existing methods despite added temporal assumption
Geometric stability across periods not thoroughly evaluated: robustness to camera pose errors, drift accumulation over many periods, and sensitivity to period boundary selection unclear
Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned despite CVPR standards; some hyperparameter choices (learning rates, decay values) lack justification
Limited statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single runs per scene make reliability assessment difficult

Technical presentation issues: temporal modulation mechanism needs more intuitive explanation; some notation inconsistencies; design choices (e.g., temporal encoding normalization range) not justified
